newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: PROFILE-Duisenberg moves towards Euro central bank. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: PROFILE-Duisenberg moves towards Euro central bank. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]

text.p: Wim Duisenberg, free-spending Dutch socialist turned hard-nosed central banker, moves a step closer this week to taking the politically-fraught helm of the single European currency.

Duisenberg, the 61-year-old Dutch central bank chief, is widely tipped as first head of the European Central Bank (ECB), a job which would give control of monetary policy under European economic and monetary union (EMU).

He takes the next step on the road to the ECB on Tuesday when he succeeds Belgian (corrects from Frenchman) Alexandre Lamfalussy as head of the Frankfurt-based European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of the ECB.
Despite his origins as a big-spending finance minister in the 1970s, Duisenberg has since earned a reputation as a successful inflation fighter as one of Europe's longest-serving central bank chiefs.
Supporters of the tall Dutchman with the bushy grey hair and ready smile say his credentials for the top position at Europe's future central bank are impeccable.

He has won backing from the inflation-fighter par excellence, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who said on Sunday that choosing Duisenberg as head of the ECB would be a signal of commitment to a stable euro.
"I believe that Mr Duisenberg really stands for lasting stability," the German central bank chief said in a radio interview.

The admiration is mutual and Duisenberg respects the Bundesbank's famous ability to resist political pressure. He once compared the German central bank with a bowl of cream: the harder you beat it, the tougher it gets.

The ECB is expected to be set up, and its head elected, after the launch members for EMU are chosen in early 1998. With the Netherlands likely to be a founder member of EMU, Duisenberg is a top candidate for the job.

Duisenberg is an enthusiastic supporter of the stability pact hammered out under the 1991 Maastricht Treaty to ensure fiscal discipline among the countries which join EMU, scheduled for launch in 1999.

Should he go to the ECB, he will need all the skills he has learnt over more than 20 years in politics and banking to negotiate the minefield of the sometimes-competing interests among up to 15 European nations.

In a 36-year career he has trodden a path from free- spending finance minister to monetarist. "It's a rather unique combination of experience," said Professor Andre Szasz, a former central bank colleague.
After working as an academic, at the International Monetary Fund and the Dutch central bank, he entered politics in 1973 as a Labour Party member of parliament.
As finance minister from 1973-77, Duisenberg allowed public spending to soar although supporters say this was due to rare circumstances prompted by the first oil price shock.
Since becoming Dutch central bank president in 1982, Duisenberg has presided over what is regarded as one of the economic success stories of the developed world.
Helped by the close link of the guilder to the mark, the Netherlands has achieved a strong currency, low inflation and interest rates, steady economic growth and falling unemployment.
In his many pronouncements on EMU, Duisenberg has been careful to stress that entry criteria must be applied strictly. But he has also warned against "fetishism" in interpreting the targets.

Duisenberg has said that whether a country can sustain a sound economic performance is more relevant than whether it precisely achieves the EMU targets for budget deficits, national debt and inflation.
Duisenberg has also been highly diplomatic in responding to questions about the challenge posed to the January 1, 1999 deadline for launching EMU.

Last month he said he assumed EMU would start on time, despite the election in France of a leftist government more intent on job creation than budgetary rectitude, and Germany's highly-publicised difficulties in cutting its budget deficit to the EMU target.
"I don't think it would make much sense to have a common currency area without Germany and France," he said.
